Do not give a dose.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"LactMed\u2019s amoxicillin entry reports these findings in breastfed infants:\\n\\n### Observed infant findings\\n- A telephone follow-up of **25 nursing mothers** recorded diarrhea in **3 infants**; the report recorded no rash or candidiasis in that group.[4] [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)\\n- In a prospective study of **40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breastmilk**, **2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash**.[6] [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)\\n- In a study comparing infants exposed to amoxicillin with infants exposed to a macrolide antibiotic, reported reactions occurred in **8.3%** of the amoxicillin-exposed infants and included **rash and somnolence**.[7] [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)\\n- A case report described recurrent generalized urticaria in a **2-month-old** after breastfeeding while the mother was receiving **amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and gentamicin**. LactMed states that the causative drug could not be determined and that the combination product was considered the most likely cause.[8] [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)\\n- A report described **mild diarrhea** in an **11-month-old** whose mother was taking amoxicillin together with acetaminophen plus codeine; the relationship was rated possible or probable.[9] [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)\\n- In a study of 25 breastfeeding mothers whose infants were older than 4 weeks, **no infant adverse effects were reported**.[3] [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)\\n\\n### Symptoms monitored in a study\\nOne controlled prospective study asked mothers to record tongue coating, feeding difficulties, stool-frequency or stool-consistency changes, diaper rash, skin rash, weight change, and jaundice. The study found no statistical differences in these parameters between infants of control mothers and infants of mothers taking the related antibiotics ampicillin or ampicillin-clavulanate.[5] [S1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2125.1991.tb05523.x)\\n\\nThis was a study measurement approach, not a separate LactMed recommendation to monitor those symptoms.\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n- Reported **amoxicillin concentrations in milk** averaged **0.69 mg/L** at 4 hours, with a range of **0.46\u20130.88 mg/L**, and **0.81 mg/L** at 5 hours, with a range of **0.39\u20131.3 mg/L**, in a study of 6 women. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)\\n- Relevant published information on **infant levels** was not found as of the LactMed revision date. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\n### Uncertainty\\nLactMed states that rash and disruption of the infant\u2019s gastrointestinal flora\u2014resulting in diarrhea or thrush\u2014have been reported, but that these effects have **not been adequately evaluated**. The reports involve different study populations, comparators, and, in the urticaria case, more than one maternal medicine; the LactMed extract does not establish that amoxicillin caused every reported symptom. The record\u2019s study count is not established in the exported data, and the extract does not provide a complete evidence inventory. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\nThe LactMed record was revised **June 15, 2026**, and the retrieved package was published **October 22, 2026**. It is a bounded extract, so absence of an additional finding in this extract is not evidence that no such finding exists. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThis LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. Omitted sections or truncation can limit the summary; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety.\\nHuman clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.\\nStopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. request.question: What does LactMed report about amoxicillin in breastfed babies? Separate observed symptoms from advice to monitor, and explain uncertainty. Do not give a dose.

response.answer:
LactMed’s amoxicillin entry reports these findings in breastfed infants:

### Observed infant findings
- A telephone follow-up of **25 nursing mothers** recorded diarrhea in **3 infants**; the report recorded no rash or candidiasis in that group.[4] [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)
- In a prospective study of **40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breastmilk**, **2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash**.[6] [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)
- In a study comparing infants exposed to amoxicillin with infants exposed to a macrolide antibiotic, reported reactions occurred in **8.3%** of the amoxicillin-exposed infants and included **rash and somnolence**.[7] [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)
- A case report described recurrent generalized urticaria in a **2-month-old** after breastfeeding while the mother was receiving **amoxicillin/clavulanic acid and gentamicin**. LactMed states that the causative drug could not be determined and that the combination product was considered the most likely cause.[8] [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)
- A report described **mild diarrhea** in an **11-month-old** whose mother was taking amoxicillin together with acetaminophen plus codeine; the relationship was rated possible or probable.[9] [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)
- In a study of 25 breastfeeding mothers whose infants were older than 4 weeks, **no infant adverse effects were reported**.[3] [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)

### Symptoms monitored in a study
One controlled prospective study asked mothers to record tongue coating, feeding difficulties, stool-frequency or stool-consistency changes, diaper rash, skin rash, weight change, and jaundice. The study found no statistical differences in these parameters between infants of control mothers and infants of mothers taking the related antibiotics ampicillin or ampicillin-clavulanate.[5] [S1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2125.1991.tb05523.x)

This was a study measurement approach, not a separate LactMed recommendation to monitor those symptoms.

### Measured exposure
- Reported **amoxicillin concentrations in milk** averaged **0.69 mg/L** at 4 hours, with a range of **0.46–0.88 mg/L**, and **0.81 mg/L** at 5 hours, with a range of **0.39–1.3 mg/L**, in a study of 6 women. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)
- Relevant published information on **infant levels** was not found as of the LactMed revision date. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

### Uncertainty
LactMed states that rash and disruption of the infant’s gastrointestinal flora—resulting in diarrhea or thrush—have been reported, but that these effects have **not been adequately evaluated**. The reports involve different study populations, comparators, and, in the urticaria case, more than one maternal medicine; the LactMed extract does not establish that amoxicillin caused every reported symptom. The record’s study count is not established in the exported data, and the extract does not provide a complete evidence inventory. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

The LactMed record was revised **June 15, 2026**, and the retrieved package was published **October 22, 2026**. It is a bounded extract, so absence of an additional finding in this extract is not evidence that no such finding exists. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

Application limits:

request.question: For sumatriptan during breastfeeding, what was measured in milk and what was actually observed in infants? If those are different kinds of evidence, explain that. No personal medication advice.

response.answer:
### Measured exposure in milk

LactMed reports these **sumatriptan milk concentrations**:

- Among five breastfeeding women who had been lactating for 11–28 weeks, the **peak milk concentration averaged 87.2 mcg/L** (range **62–113 mcg/L**), occurring at about **2.5 hours**; the reported mean milk half-life was **2.2 hours**. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8866921/)
- In a separate report of seven women at least one month postpartum, peak milk concentrations averaged **59.3 mcg/L** (range **24.6–112.8 mcg/L**) at **2–4 hours**; the average milk concentration was **23.2 mcg/L** (range **7.7–50.6 mcg/L**), with a reported mean milk half-life of **4.9 hours**. [S2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33730376/)

**Infant-level measurements:** LactMed states that relevant published information on **infant levels** was not found as of the record’s revision date. The retrieved record does not establish an infant specimen type or provide infant drug concentrations. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

### What was observed in infants

LactMed reports correspondence with the manufacturer concerning **three women** who used sumatriptan while breastfeeding; **none reported adverse effects in their infants**. The exposure amount and route were unspecified. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

These are different evidence types: milk concentrations are **measured exposure data**, whereas the infant information is a limited report of **reported clinical observations**. The infant observations do not provide infant drug levels, and the milk measurements do not by themselves establish infant outcomes or safety. The retrieved LactMed extract is bounded, and its study count is not established from the extract. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

Application limits:
This LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. Omitted sections or truncation can limit the summary; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

[S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)\\n\\nThe label\u2019s **Adverse Reactions** section reports gastrointestinal reactions and other reactions in adults with type 2 diabetes, including diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, indigestion, abdominal discomfort, headache, hypoglycemia, rash, and dyspnea. In another group, metformin was undetectable in infant serum at **<5 mcg/L**. Some infant ages and extent of nursing were not stated. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\nLactMed reports that:\\n\\n- Seven infants aged 5\u201325 months were judged healthy, with growth and development progressing as expected; two had normal Denver Developmental Screening tests.\\n- Three infants had no detectable adverse effects attributed to metformin.\\n- In three young breastfed infants, no low blood glucose was reported, and their mothers reported no adverse reactions.\\n- In a study of infants who were predominantly breastfed or formula-fed, no differences were found at the reported follow-up points in height, weight, motor-social development, or rates of illness.\\n\\nThese are findings from separate cited reports and study populations, not a single combined study result. request.question: Compare metformin label warnings for the adult taking it with findings in breastfed infants. Identify which source says what, and disclose missing sections. Don't give any doses.

response.answer:
## Source identity

The retrieved medication was **metformin**. The adult label was specifically **“METFORMIN HCL TABLET [QPHARMA, INC.]”**; the exact product or formulation was not confirmed. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

## Adult label: what it says

The DailyMed label’s **Warnings** section describes lactic acidosis as a rare, serious complication and discusses higher-risk clinical contexts including renal impairment, hypoperfusion or hypoxemia, heart failure, hepatic disease, dehydration, sepsis, age, and alcohol exposure. These warnings concern the **person taking metformin**, not breastfed infants. The retrieved Warnings text was truncated. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

The label’s **Adverse Reactions** section reports gastrointestinal reactions and other reactions in adults with type 2 diabetes, including diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, indigestion, abdominal discomfort, headache, hypoglycemia, rash, and dyspnea. These are adult label findings, not infant outcomes. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

The label’s **lactation section** raises a potential concern about hypoglycemia in nursing infants. That is a label warning, not an observed infant outcome in the retrieved label. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)

## LactMed: breastfed-infant evidence

LactMed reports measured exposure and observed infant findings separately. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

### Measured exposure

Reported **milk metformin concentrations** included:

- **270 mcg/L** as an average over 24 hours in one group.
- Approximately **380 mcg/L** in one sample collected about 4–5 hours after administration.
- **130 and 270 mcg/L** as average milk levels in two women over 72 hours.
- **130–270 mcg/L** as average levels in another group.
- **410 mcg/L** as an average milk level in a postpartum study.

Infant-level information was also retrieved: LactMed reports **infant serum** measurements, including undetectable results below the assay thresholds and measured concentrations of **50 and 80 mcg/L** in two infants. In another group, metformin was undetectable in infant serum at **<5 mcg/L**. Some infant ages and extent of nursing were not stated. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)

### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reports that:

- Seven infants aged 5–25 months were judged healthy, with growth and development progressing as expected; two had normal Denver Developmental Screening tests.
- Three infants had no detectable adverse effects attributed to metformin.
- In three young breastfed infants, no low blood glucose was reported, and their mothers reported no adverse reactions.
- In a study of infants who were predominantly breastfed or formula-fed, no differences were found at the reported follow-up points in height, weight, motor-social development, or rates of illness.

These are findings from separate cited reports and study populations, not a single combined study result. LactMed’s returned extract does not establish a study count; its ten reference entries are not a study count. Relevant citations listed by LactMed include [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12436333/), [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12545145/), [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15384618/), [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15932841/), and [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16737874/). The individual article abstracts were not separately retrieved here, so these findings are reported from LactMed’s summaries rather than from independent abstract review.

## Comparison

| Topic | Adult label | Breastfed-infant evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Serious warning | Lactic acidosis warning for the person taking metformin. | No corresponding infant lactic-acidosis outcome was reported in the retrieved LactMed extract. |
| Hypoglycemia | Adult adverse-reaction listing includes hypoglycemia. | The label raises a potential infant hypoglycemia concern; LactMed reports no low blood glucose in one group of three infants. These are different source statements and populations. |
| Gastrointestinal and other adult reactions | Reported in adults with type 2 diabetes. | The retrieved LactMed infant sections do not report those adult reactions as infant outcomes. |
| Drug exposure | The label discusses metformin treatment in the medicine-taker population. | LactMed reports measured metformin in milk and, in some cases, infant serum. Exposure measurements are not clinical outcomes. |

## Missing and limited sections

- The DailyMed extract identified **`warnings_and_precautions`** and **`boxed_warning`** as missing. The source states that absent sections may not apply or may be absent from the source; this is not proof that no related information exists. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)
- The DailyMed **Warnings** text was truncated. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)
- The exact DailyMed product/formulation was not confirmed. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551)
- LactMed returned all four expected sections without truncation, but some study details—including certain infant ages, extent of nursing, timing, and the overall study count—were missing or not established in the extract. [S23](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501020/)
- The label’s former “Pregnancy Category B” wording is historical; FDA pregnancy letter categories are not current classifications. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=06ade2e1-5981-4e3d-b7e9-7ff083eb4551) [S22](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule)

Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks; discuss treatment changes with the prescribing clinician.

request.question: Is there an FDA-listed pregnancy exposure registry covering topiramate? Give the listing and registry contact or enrollment link if returned, and distinguish finding a registry from being eligible to enroll.

response.answer:
Yes. The FDA directory lists **The North American Antiepileptic Drug in Pregnancy Registry** for **Topamax, Trokendi XR, and Qudexy XR (topiramate)**. It is listed as **ongoing**. [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

- **Enrollment:** [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)
- **Contact:** Massachusetts General Hospital for Children; toll-free **1-888-233-2334**. [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

This listing does **not** establish individual eligibility. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability; this lookup did not determine either. The FDA directory also states that its list is not comprehensive and that FDA does not operate or endorse the listed registries. [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

request.question: Find up to two recruiting ADHD studies involving children in the United States. Include exact study links, overall and site status if present, update dates, contacts and qualification limits. Do not decide whether a child qualifies.

response.answer:
## Recruiting U.S. ADHD studies involving children

The search returned two potential matches. These are directory listings, not recommendations. The study team must confirm current site availability and eligibility; this lookup does not determine whether a child qualifies. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

### 1. Virtual-reality interventions related to ADHD — NCT05608434

**Exact study link:** [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05608434)

- **Overall status:** RECRUITING
- **Study type:** INTERVENTIONAL
- **Source population field:** Not established in the returned record; the registry age fields list children aged 8–16 years. The search’s requested child band was 2 to under 12 years, so the returned age range only partly overlaps that search band.
- **Last update posted:** 2026-11-12
- **Recruiting site:** NIH Clinical Center, Bethesda, Maryland — **RECRUITING**
- **Contacts:**
  - Saadia A. Choudhury — (301) 437-0489; saadia.choudhury@nih.gov
  - Daniel S. Pine, M.D. — (301) 594-1318; daniel.pine@nih.gov
  - NIH Office of Patient Recruitment — 800-411-1222; TTY 711; ccopr@nih.gov
- **Qualification limits listed:** Parent consent and child assent; age limits; ADHD diagnosis or a specified impairing inattention presentation; screening assessments; availability for study procedures and travel to the NIH Clinical Center; and exclusions involving certain cognitive, neurological, psychiatric, visual, prior-intervention, and investigator-assessed circumstances. The pilot and main trial have different medication-related criteria. Review the full criteria with the study team.

### 2. SPN-812 (viloxazine extended-release) in preschool-age children with ADHD — NCT04781140

**Exact study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04781140)

- **Overall status:** RECRUITING
- **Study type:** INTERVENTIONAL
- **Source population field:** Not established in the returned record; the registry age fields list children aged 48–69 months.
- **Last update posted:** 2026-10-05
- **Returned site statuses:** Both RECRUITING and non-recruiting sites were listed. Examples of **RECRUITING** sites include:
  - The Center for Clinical Trials, Inc., Saraland, Alabama
  - Preferred Research Partners, Inc., Little Rock, Arkansas
  - Advanced Research Center, Anaheim, California
  - Sun Valley Research Center, Imperial, California
  - Alliance Research, Long Beach, California
  - Multiple sites in Colorado and Florida
- **Central contact:** Olivia Elbaum — 301-838-2500; clinicaltrials@supernus.com
- **Example site contacts:**
  - Saraland, Alabama — 251-341-7021; info@thecenterforclinicaltrials.com
  - Little Rock, Arkansas — 501-553-9987; info@preferredresearchpartners.com
  - Anaheim, California — 714-999-6688; contact@arctrials.com
  - Imperial, California — 760-545-0123; svrcinfo@sunvalleyb.com
- **Qualification limits listed:** Age limits; parent or guardian consent; ADHD diagnosis confirmed through the study’s assessment process; symptom-severity and functional assessments; participation in a structured group activity; and restrictions involving certain medical, neurological, psychiatric, cardiovascular, medication, investigational-drug, allergy, and behavioral-treatment circumstances. The returned location list is truncated, so it is not a complete site listing.

The registry notes that overall recruitment does not mean every location is recruiting, and the returned search was limited to the first 20 API matches with literal ADHD-related terms; synonyms may have been missed. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

Application limits:
The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Are any recruiting pediatric epilepsy studies returned for Canada? Show up to two with study links and contacts, or clearly explain if the search found none. Do not substitute completed studies.

response.answer:
One **RECRUITING** Canadian study was returned; no completed studies were substituted. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=pediatric+epilepsy+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=Canada)

### Real World Evidence on the Use of Medical Cannabis in Pediatrics — NCT05863910
- **Study type:** OBSERVATIONAL
- **Conditions:** Cancer, Epilepsy, Neurodevelopmental Disorders
- **Location:** U Manitoba, Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada — site status: **RECRUITING**
- **Age range:** 3–17 years
- **Study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910)
- **Contact:** Lauren E. Kelly, PhD  
  - Phone: 204-272-3149  
  - Email: lauren.kelly@umanitoba.ca

The registry’s epilepsy match is **indirect or unverified**: “epilepsy” appears in the conditions list, but clinical suitability for the requested pediatric epilepsy population was not confirmed. The eligibility text includes authorization for medical cannabis for seizures. [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910)

The search returned no second study. This was a bounded search using literal topic words; synonyms may have been missed. The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability; this lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation. Application limits:

request.question: Where is the official FDA page a parent can use to report a possible medication problem? Does a report by itself show that the medicine caused the problem? Please don't ask me for identifying information or file anything.

response.answer:
The official FDA page is **FDA MedWatch: report a suspected medicine problem**: [S3](https://www.fda.gov/safety/medwatch-fda-safety-information-and-adverse-event-reporting-program)

A report by itself does **not** establish that the medicine caused the problem; the retrieved source describes it as a suspected problem report and states that it does not establish causation. [S3](https://www.fda.gov/safety/medwatch-fda-safety-information-and-adverse-event-reporting-program)

No report was filed, and no identifying information was requested.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Find a PubMed paper about levetiracetam while breastfeeding, retrieve its abstract, and summarize only the study design, population and findings actually available. Distinguish drug exposure from infant outcomes.

response.answer:
**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?* [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Study design and population
- The abstract does not state a formal study-design label. It reports that breastfeeding women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam completed a questionnaire and provided serial breast-milk samples from before dosing through 12 hours afterward, plus one pre-dose maternal serum sample.
- The study included **20 women and 21 infants**; one woman had twins. Sixteen infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Drug exposure
- Levetiracetam concentrations were measured in breast milk and maternal serum.
- The reported trough breast-milk/serum ratio was **0.98 ± 0.20**.
- The abstract reports infant exposure estimates and relative infant-dose values separately for fully and partially breastfed infants; these are study findings, not dosing instructions.
- Correlations were reported among levetiracetam dose, maternal serum concentrations, breast-milk trough concentrations and breast-milk AUC values. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Infant outcomes
- Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants; the abstract states that this resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding.
- The abstract states that all infants gained weight according to age.

{"answer": "**Paper:** *Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?* [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Study design and population
- The abstract does not state a formal study-design label. It reports that breastfeeding women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam completed a questionnaire and provided serial breast-milk samples from before dosing through 12 hours afterward, plus one pre-dose maternal serum sample.
- The study included **20 women and 21 infants**; one woman had twins. Sixteen infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Drug exposure
- Levetiracetam concentrations were measured in breast milk and maternal serum.
- The reported trough breast-milk/serum ratio was **0.98 ± 0.20**.
- The abstract reports infant exposure estimates and relative infant-dose values separately for fully and partially breastfed infants; these are study findings, not dosing instructions.
- Correlations were reported among levetiracetam dose, maternal serum concentrations, breast-milk trough concentrations and breast-milk AUC values. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

### Infant outcomes
- Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants; the abstract states that this resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding.
- The abstract states that all infants gained weight according to age.
- The abstract does not establish that levetiracetam caused the reported somnolence; it reports the authors’ statement that the reports could be related to breast-milk exposure. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

request.question: What can infant adverse-event reports involving acetaminophen tell a researcher, and what can they not establish about how often side effects occur or whether the medicine caused them? Use the MCP and state the age scope actually queried.

response.answer:
### Age scope queried

The MCP queried acetaminophen FAERS reports for patients whose age was coded **in months from 0 through 12**. Other age-unit encodings were excluded. The returned results were a bounded top-25 reaction-term extract, not a complete infant dataset. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

### What the reports can tell a researcher

They can describe which terms appeared most frequently in this queried report subset. Examples included:

- Vomiting: **117 reports**
- Pyrexia: **98**
- Rash: **60**
- Irritability: **42**
- Seizure: **35**
- Acute hepatic failure: **28**
- Liver injury: **28**

The extract also included use- and administration-related terms, including off-label use, administration error, overdose, and product-use issues. For each returned term, the source population and confirmed age band were listed as **not established**; the query filter itself did not confirm those details. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

### What the reports cannot establish

These are **FAERS reporting counts**, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes. The query had no exposure denominator, so it cannot establish how often side effects occur, calculate incidence, or estimate risk. The results cannot be generalized to all infants or to everyone exposed to acetaminophen. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)

They also cannot establish that acetaminophen caused any reported event. The MCP result states that spontaneous reports do not establish causation. A term absent from this bounded extract would not establish that the event did not occur or was not reported. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=25)[S2](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

The MCP identity lookup matched the queried ingredient as acetaminophen, but that lookup does not change the FAERS limitations. [S3](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/161/properties.json)

Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks; treatment changes belong in a prescribing-clinician conversation.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

[S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/)\\n- In a study of 26 women with extensive 24-hour milk and serum sampling, mean milk sertraline concentration was **129 mcg/L** (range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**) and mean norsertraline concentration was **258 mcg/L** (range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**). [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)\\n- One study reported **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk; samples were collected 13 hours after administration.\\n- In one woman, sertraline was below the breast-milk quantification limit of **<5 mcg/L**. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThe LactMed **Drug Levels** section was truncated, so the concentration list is not a complete record. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)\\n- **25 breastfed infants followed through six months:** reported six-month weight gain was within national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal infant effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)\\n- **One 4-month-old infant:** benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation were reported. The returned extract does not establish that sertraline caused these findings.\\n- **One preterm infant born at 33 weeks:** hyperthermia, altered muscle tone, and high-pitched crying were reported after exposure through breastfeeding. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)\\n- **A study of infants exposed to an SSRI during pregnancy, with or without breastfeeding exposure:** blunted pain responses were reported compared with the study\u2019s control group. request.question: Using the parent medication information tool, summarize the sertraline evidence from LactMed and the product label. Separate measured milk exposure from observed infant outcomes. Include links and questions to ask a clinician. Do not give dosing or medication decisions.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during breastfeeding

The retrieved evidence includes a LactMed record and one selected DailyMed product label. The DailyMed label is for **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, effective **November 5, 2026**; the exact product match was not confirmed. The label’s lactation section was returned, but its warnings, boxed-warning, drug-interaction, and related sections were missing from the extract. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Measured exposure

LactMed reported the following **milk concentrations**:

- In a pooled analysis of 15 mothers, mean breast-milk sertraline concentration was **45 mcg/L**, with a range of **7–207 mcg/L**. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/)
- In a study of 26 women with extensive 24-hour milk and serum sampling, mean milk sertraline concentration was **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**) and mean norsertraline concentration was **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**). [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- At 2 months postpartum, four mothers had mean milk concentrations of **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline; samples were collected at random times after the previous administration.
- In one case involving a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline across three randomly timed sampling days. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- One study reported **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk; samples were collected 13 hours after administration.
- In one woman, sertraline was below the breast-milk quantification limit of **<5 mcg/L**. In eight other women, milk concentrations ranged from **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**.
- In six women providing random milk samples, the median sertraline concentration was **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**).
- In 15 mothers providing timed milk samples, the mean concentration was **87 mcg/L** (range **12–288 mcg/L**).

These are research measurements, not dosing instructions. The returned LactMed extract did **not** include a complete infant-level concentration section: infant-level numeric information is therefore **not available in the returned extract**. LactMed’s summary states that sertraline is usually not detected in infant serum and that norsertraline may be detectable at low levels in infant serum, but the infant-level specimen details and numeric results were not fully returned. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The LactMed **Drug Levels** section was truncated, so the concentration list is not a complete record. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reported findings from separate study populations:

- **26 breastfed infants:** no detectable acute adverse reactions were observed in the cited study. The study population and exposure findings are reported in the LactMed extract. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- **14 mother–infant pairs:** infant whole-blood serotonin levels were measured before and after maternal treatment; the reported infant averages were similar, and no adverse effects were reported in those infants. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)
- **25 breastfed infants followed through six months:** reported six-month weight gain was within national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal infant effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)
- **One 4-month-old infant:** benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation were reported. The returned extract does not establish that sertraline caused these findings.
- **One preterm infant born at 33 weeks:** hyperthermia, altered muscle tone, and high-pitched crying were reported after exposure through breastfeeding. The case report also reported measurable sertraline and metabolite concentrations in the infant specimen, but the returned LactMed extract does not provide the full infant-level measurement details. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- **A study of infants exposed to an SSRI during pregnancy, with or without breastfeeding exposure:** blunted pain responses were reported compared with the study’s control group. Four of the 30 exposed infants were exposed to sertraline; the returned extract states that the control group did not include depressed, unmedicated mothers, so the specific contribution of sertraline was not established. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)

The returned **Effects in Breastfed Infants** section was truncated; these observations do not represent a complete list of reported infant findings. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Product-label evidence

The selected DailyMed label states that published literature shows low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk. In a pooled analysis of **53 mother–infant pairs**, exclusively human-milk-fed infants had average sertraline serum levels equal to **2%** of the maternal serum levels, with a reported range of **0–15%**; the label states that no adverse reactions were observed in those infants. This is label-reported exposure and outcome information, not an individualized safety determination. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The label’s returned adult adverse-reaction section lists hypersensitivity reactions, serotonin syndrome, increased bleeding risk, activation of mania or hypomania, discontinuation syndrome, seizures, angle-closure glaucoma, hyponatremia, and sexual dysfunction, among other listed reactions. These are findings and warnings for the medicine-taker label population, not automatically observed effects in a breastfed infant. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Questions to ask a clinician or pharmacist

- Does the selected DailyMed label match the exact product and formulation?
- How closely do the reported study populations match this lactation context, including the infant’s age and prematurity status?
- Which findings are measured milk or infant exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
- What infant-level information is missing because the LactMed extract is truncated?
- What uncertainties remain about the effects of the underlying condition and its treatment?
- What follow-up information would be relevant for the lactating person and infant?
- Which findings, if any, require professional assessment in this specific situation?
- If treatment is changed, how should continuity of care be handled? Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and belongs in a prescribing-clinician conversation.

Sources: [LactMed](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) · [DailyMed label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32) [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32) · [MedlinePlus: Sertraline](https://medlineplus.gov/druginfo/meds/a697048.html?utm_source=mplusconnect&utm_medium=service) [S8](https://medlineplus.gov/druginfo/meds/a697048.html?utm_source=mplusconnect&utm_medium=service)

Application limits:
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

Do not provide medication decisions or doses.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Sertraline during lactation: evidence brief\\n\\n**Identity:** The medication-evidence lookup matched **sertraline** exactly as a single ingredient. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)\\n\\n### Effects on the lactating person\\n\\n- LactMed reports observations of decreased milk supply after starting sertraline in six patients; maternal doses were not reported. One patient reported increased supply after stopping and decreased supply after restarting, but this is a single reported observation and does not establish causation. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- A small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor exposure\u2014including one participant taking sertraline\u2014reported delayed lactogenesis II compared with controls, while the extract states that feeding difficulties after postpartum day 4 did not differ statistically. This was not a sertraline-only study. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The selected DailyMed label states that published data show low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk and that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. The selected label was **\u201cSERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]\u201d**, effective November 5, 2026; this was one selected product label, not all formulations. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n\\nRetrieved LactMed milk-concentration findings included:\\n\\n- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**; range **7\u2013207 mcg/L** in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a study of 26 breastfeeding women, milk sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L**; range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**. Norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L**; range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- At two months postpartum, average milk concentrations in four mothers were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a case involving a preterm infant, breastmilk sertraline and norsertraline averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively, at random sampling times. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- One report found **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk, sampled 13 hours after exposure. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- Other reported milk measurements included **<5 mcg/L** in one woman, **11.1\u201324.5 mcg/L** in eight women, a median of **11.3 mcg/L** in six women, and an average of **87 mcg/L** with a range of **12\u2013288 mcg/L** in another study. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThese are research concentration measurements, not personal dosing guidance. The returned LactMed extract did **not** include an infant-level concentration excerpt; infant-level information was therefore incomplete in that extract. A separately retrieved PubMed abstract reported detectable concentrations of sertraline in three nursing infants and desmethylsertraline in six, using **infant serum** as the specimen, with detected infant serum concentrations below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\n- LactMed reports benign neonatal sleep myoclonus in one 4-month-old infant and spontaneously resolving agitation in that case passage. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The extract reports several small groups in which no acute adverse reactions or other adverse effects were observed during the reported study periods. These observations do not establish that unaddressed outcomes were absent. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In one case involving a preterm infant born at 33 weeks, the reported outcomes included hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation disorders, and high-pitched crying. The case also reported infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite and later reported dissipation of symptoms and decreased serum levels after breastfeeding was discontinued. The source\u2019s attribution was a case-report interpretation; this single case should not be generalized beyond its reported population. [S30](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)\\n- Another passage describes sedation in an infant whose mother was also taking zopiclone and occasional alprazolam; the co-exposures are part of that source record. [S29](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22504099/)\\n- A pain-response study included four sertraline-exposed infants among 30 infants exposed to an SSRI. The source stated that the comparison group did not include depressed, nonmedicated mothers, so the role of maternal depression-related factors was not resolved. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)\\n\\nThe returned **Effects in Breastfed Infants** section was truncated, including an incomplete passage from a case involving sertraline with methylphenidate. The missing text cannot be reconstructed from this lookup. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### FAERS report-only context\\n\\nFor the broad queried sertraline report set, the returned top terms and counts were: nausea **14,075**; \u201cdrug ineffective\u201d **13,855**; fatigue **13,021**; headache **11,284**; anxiety **10,530**; diarrhoea **10,499**; dizziness **9,741**; and depression **9,612**. The returned cohort scope was reports matching the query, not a complete exposed population; the source population was not established. These counts are reporting volume, not incidence, confirmed outcomes, or proof of causation, and cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)[S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)\\n\\n### Missing-evidence and retrieval limitations\\n\\n- The LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated; the extract is not complete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The PubMed search was bounded and not a systematic review. Five records were requested; abstract text was retrieved for three. No abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**. This is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the studies or relevant research do not exist. Titles alone were not used for outcome claims. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)[S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)[S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)\\n- Some retrieved studies concerned SSRIs or antidepressants as groups, did not specify the individual drug, or included mixed exposures. Those findings were not treated as sertraline-specific.\\n- Study counts were not established from the LactMed extract; reference counts are not study counts. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The selected DailyMed label\u2019s standalone adult warning sections for warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions were missing from the returned extract. Missing sections do not establish absence of information. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n\\n### Questions to ask your clinician or pharmacist\\n\\n1. Does this evidence apply to my exact formulation and all active ingredients?\\n2. Which retrieved findings concern measured milk or infant exposure, and which concern observed infant outcomes?\\n3. How closely do the study populations match my infant\u2019s age, feeding pattern, and prematurity status?\\n4. Do the co-exposures in any reported case resemble medicines being used in my situation?\\n5. What uncertainties or missing evidence should we discuss before making a treatment decision?\\n6. What follow-up information should be discussed with the prescribing clinician or pharmacist?\\n\\nThe retrieved MCP guidance states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and belongs in a prescribing-clinician conversation.\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThese FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.\\nHuman clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.\\nStopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. ## Sertraline during lactation: evidence brief

**Identity:** The medication-evidence lookup matched **sertraline** exactly as a single ingredient. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Effects on the lactating person

- LactMed reports observations of decreased milk supply after starting sertraline in six patients; maternal doses were not reported. One patient reported increased supply after stopping and decreased supply after restarting, but this is a single reported observation and does not establish causation. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor exposure—including one participant taking sertraline—reported delayed lactogenesis II compared with controls, while the extract states that feeding difficulties after postpartum day 4 did not differ statistically. This was not a sertraline-only study. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The selected DailyMed label states that published data show low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk and that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. The selected label was **“SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]”**, effective November 5, 2026; this was one selected product label, not all formulations. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Measured exposure

Retrieved LactMed milk-concentration findings included:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**; range **7–207 mcg/L** in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of 26 breastfeeding women, milk sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L**; range **11–938 mcg/L**. Norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L**; range **20–1,498 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- At two months postpartum, average milk concentrations in four mothers were **26.4 mcg/L** for sertraline and **29 mcg/L** for norsertraline. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a case involving a preterm infant, breastmilk sertraline and norsertraline averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively, at random sampling times. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- One report found **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk, sampled 13 hours after exposure. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Other reported milk measurements included **<5 mcg/L** in one woman, **11.1–24.5 mcg/L** in eight women, a median of **11.3 mcg/L** in six women, and an average of **87 mcg/L** with a range of **12–288 mcg/L** in another study. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These are research concentration measurements, not personal dosing guidance. The returned LactMed extract did **not** include an infant-level concentration excerpt; infant-level information was therefore incomplete in that extract. A separately retrieved PubMed abstract reported detectable concentrations of sertraline in three nursing infants and desmethylsertraline in six, using **infant serum** as the specimen, with detected infant serum concentrations below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

### Observed infant outcomes

- LactMed reports benign neonatal sleep myoclonus in one 4-month-old infant and spontaneously resolving agitation in that case passage. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The extract reports several small groups in which no acute adverse reactions or other adverse effects were observed during the reported study periods. These observations do not establish that unaddressed outcomes were absent. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In one case involving a preterm infant born at 33 weeks, the reported outcomes included hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation disorders, and high-pitched crying. The case also reported infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite and later reported dissipation of symptoms and decreased serum levels after breastfeeding was discontinued. The source’s attribution was a case-report interpretation; this single case should not be generalized beyond its reported population. [S30](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- Another passage describes sedation in an infant whose mother was also taking zopiclone and occasional alprazolam; the co-exposures are part of that source record. [S29](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22504099/)
- A pain-response study included four sertraline-exposed infants among 30 infants exposed to an SSRI. The source stated that the comparison group did not include depressed, nonmedicated mothers, so the role of maternal depression-related factors was not resolved. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)

The returned **Effects in Breastfed Infants** section was truncated, including an incomplete passage from a case involving sertraline with methylphenidate. The missing text cannot be reconstructed from this lookup. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### FAERS report-only context

For the broad queried sertraline report set, the returned top terms and counts were: nausea **14,075**; “drug ineffective” **13,855**; fatigue **13,021**; headache **11,284**; anxiety **10,530**; diarrhoea **10,499**; dizziness **9,741**; and depression **9,612**. The returned cohort scope was reports matching the query, not a complete exposed population; the source population was not established. These counts are reporting volume, not incidence, confirmed outcomes, or proof of causation, and cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)[S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Missing-evidence and retrieval limitations

- The LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated; the extract is not complete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The PubMed search was bounded and not a systematic review. Five records were requested; abstract text was retrieved for three. No abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**. This is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the studies or relevant research do not exist. Titles alone were not used for outcome claims. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)[S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)[S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)
- Some retrieved studies concerned SSRIs or antidepressants as groups, did not specify the individual drug, or included mixed exposures. Those findings were not treated as sertraline-specific.
- Study counts were not established from the LactMed extract; reference counts are not study counts. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The selected DailyMed label’s standalone adult warning sections for warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions were missing from the returned extract. Missing sections do not establish absence of information. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Questions to ask your clinician or pharmacist

1. Does this evidence apply to my exact formulation and all active ingredients?
2. Which retrieved findings concern measured milk or infant exposure, and which concern observed infant outcomes?
3. How closely do the study populations match my infant’s age, feeding pattern, and prematurity status?
4. Do the co-exposures in any reported case resemble medicines being used in my situation?
5. What uncertainties or missing evidence should we discuss before making a treatment decision?
6. What follow-up information should be discussed with the prescribing clinician or pharmacist?

The retrieved MCP guidance states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and belongs in a prescribing-clinician conversation.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

These are counts of extracted passages, not studies or proven effects. Context-only passages and gap statements are counted separately. Empty rows do not establish absence of evidence elsewhere or safety. This inventory does not replace the cited findings or validate applicability.

The returned cohort scope was reports matching the query, not a complete exposed population; the source population was not established. These counts are reporting volume, not incidence, confirmed outcomes, or proof of causation, and cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8)[S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Missing-evidence and retrieval limitations

- The LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated; the extract is not complete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The PubMed search was bounded and not a systematic review. Five records were requested; abstract text was retrieved for three. No abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**. This is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the studies or relevant research do not exist. Titles alone were not used for outcome claims. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)[S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/)[S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)
- Some retrieved studies concerned SSRIs or antidepressants as groups, did not specify the individual drug, or included mixed exposures. Those findings were not treated as sertraline-specific.
- Study counts were not established from the LactMed extract; reference counts are not study counts. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The selected DailyMed label’s standalone adult warning sections for warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions were missing from the returned extract. Missing sections do not establish absence of information. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Questions to ask your clinician or pharmacist

1. Does this evidence apply to my exact formulation and all active ingredients?
2. Which retrieved findings concern measured milk or infant exposure, and which concern observed infant outcomes?
3. How closely do the study populations match my infant’s age, feeding pattern, and prematurity status?
4. Do the co-exposures in any reported case resemble medicines being used in my situation?
5. What uncertainties or missing evidence should we discuss before making a treatment decision?
6. What follow-up information should be discussed with the prescribing clinician or pharmacist?

The retrieved MCP guidance states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and belongs in a prescribing-clinician conversation.

These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.

request.question: Please prepare questions for my clinician about the evidence for sertraline during breastfeeding. Use the evidence brief tool.

response.answer:
## Questions to ask your clinician

### Applying the evidence
- Does the available evidence apply to my exact sertraline product and formulation?
- How closely do the studies match my infant’s age, health, prematurity status, and extent of breastfeeding?
- Which findings are measured drug exposure, and which are observed infant outcomes?
- What limitations should I consider because some evidence comes from small studies, case reports, or mixed SSRI populations?

### Measured exposure
- How should the reported milk concentrations be interpreted for my situation?
- What does it mean that the retrieved studies measured sertraline and/or norsertraline in milk at values including **45 mcg/L (range 7–207)**, **129 mcg/L (range 11–938)**, **258 mcg/L (range 20–1,498)**, **26.4 mcg/L**, **29 mcg/L**, **201 mcg/L**, **358 mcg/L**, **26 mcg/L**, **46 mcg/L**, **<5 mcg/L**, **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L (range 3.6–35.7)**, and **87 mcg/L (range 12–288)**? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The retrieved LactMed extract did not include an infant-level concentration passage in its returned measurement section. Does the underlying study provide infant-level results relevant to this situation? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- How should milk-sampling timing and the reported foremilk/hindmilk differences affect interpretation? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes
- Which infant findings were directly observed in sertraline-exposure studies, and which were not established by the retrieved extract?
- How relevant are the reported findings from full-term versus preterm infants to my infant?
- Does the evidence distinguish exposure through breastmilk alone from exposure during pregnancy plus breastfeeding?
- What evidence exists about longer-term infant growth or development, and what remains uncertain? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

### Lactation and maternal effects
- What does the evidence actually show about milk production or breastfeeding outcomes, separate from drug concentrations in milk?
- How should we interpret the LactMed reports of decreased milk supply in six patients and the mixed SSRI breastfeeding studies? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Could the underlying condition or pregnancy exposure explain some breastfeeding outcomes reported in observational studies, rather than sertraline alone? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Follow-up and uncertainty
- What additional information about my infant or my formulation would change how you interpret this evidence?
- What follow-up, if any, would you recommend for evaluating feeding, growth, or development?
- Which uncertainties are most important to discuss before making a treatment decision?
- Should we involve a pharmacist, pediatric clinician, or lactation professional in reviewing the evidence?

### Evidence-retrieval limitations
- The LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated in the retrieved extract, so the record is incomplete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The bounded PubMed search returned abstract text for three of five requested records; no abstract text was returned for **PMIDs 38133585 and 32320387**. That is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the studies or other research do not exist. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)
- A sertraline review’s abstract described sertraline as generally recommended in postpartum care, but that is a source statement and does not determine an individual treatment decision. [S48](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38811474/)

**Continuity-of-care question:** “If treatment changes are being considered, what risks of changing treatment should we weigh alongside the breastfeeding evidence?”

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.
PubMed abstract coverage: abstract text was retrieved for 3 of 5 requested PMIDs. No abstract text was returned for PMID(s): 38133585, 32320387. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that a study or research does not exist. Titles alone are not outcome evidence.
Structured evidence rows (retrieval inventory)
| Evidence axis | Extracted findings | Context-only passages | Gap statements |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Effect on the pregnant or lactating person | 19 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 0 | 0 |
| Measured transfer or exposure to fetus or infant | 31 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 0 | 0 |
| Observed outcomes in fetus or infant | 24 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 0 | 2 |
These are counts of extracted passages, not studies or proven effects. Context-only passages and gap statements are counted separately. Empty rows do not establish absence of evidence elsewhere or safety. This inventory does not replace the cited findings or validate applicability.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

- How should we interpret the LactMed reports of decreased milk supply in six patients and the mixed SSRI breastfeeding studies? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Could the underlying condition or pregnancy exposure explain some breastfeeding outcomes reported in observational studies, rather than sertraline alone? [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Follow-up and uncertainty
- What additional information about my infant or my formulation would change how you interpret this evidence?
- What follow-up, if any, would you recommend for evaluating feeding, growth, or development?
- Which uncertainties are most important to discuss before making a treatment decision?
- Should we involve a pharmacist, pediatric clinician, or lactation professional in reviewing the evidence?

### Evidence-retrieval limitations
- The LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated in the retrieved extract, so the record is incomplete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The bounded PubMed search returned abstract text for three of five requested records; no abstract text was returned for **PMIDs 38133585 and 32320387**. That is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the studies or other research do not exist. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)

**Continuity-of-care question:** “If treatment changes are being considered, what risks of changing treatment should we weigh alongside the breastfeeding evidence?”

These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.

## Pregnancy evidence brief: daridorexant

**Identity:** The retrieved identity match was daridorexant (RxCUI 2591497). [S15](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/2591497/properties.json)

### Evidence axes

| Requested axis | Retrieved evidence |
|---|---|
| **Effects on the pregnant person** | **Empty.** No human maternal pregnancy-effect findings were retrieved. The product label states that there are no available data in pregnant women to evaluate drug-associated risks of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |
| **Measured fetal or infant exposure** | **Empty.** No measured fetal or infant exposure data were retrieved. |
| **Observed fetal or infant outcomes** | **Empty for human observed outcomes.** The label contains animal findings: in pregnant rats and rabbits, the cited studies reported no fetal toxicity or malformation; in rabbits, decreased maternal weight gain and food consumption were reported at the highest tested animal exposure. These are animal findings, not human pregnancy outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) |

Empty rows reflect the retrieved extract and are not evidence of safety or proof that no evidence exists elsewhere.

### Maternal pharmacokinetic data

**No maternal pregnancy pharmacokinetic data were retrieved.** The label’s Pregnancy Clinical Considerations section contained no maternal pharmacokinetic data, and the pregnancy-focused PubMed pharmacokinetic query returned no records. The empty query result is not proof of drug identity, safety, or absence of evidence elsewhere. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22daridorexant%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22daridorexant%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22daridorexant%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29+AND+%28%22Pharmacokinetics%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Drug+Elimination+Routes%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pharmacokinetic%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+clearance%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22area+under+the+curve%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22dose+adjustment%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=3&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

The pregnancy PubMed query returned three records:

- [PMID 36630580](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630580/) [S14](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630580/)
- [PMID 36630579](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630579/) [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630579/)
- [PMID 35802843](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35802843/) [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35802843/)

No abstract text was returned for any of the three records. Titles alone were not used to describe study outcomes. The search was bounded and not a systematic review. [S8](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22daridorexant%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22daridorexant%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22daridorexant%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
