[S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n**Underlying-condition context:** The pregnancy label states that epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-drug exposure, has been associated with several maternal and obstetric outcomes. This is disease-context information, not a lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n### Fetal exposure\\n\\nNo quantitative maternal-to-fetal lamotrigine concentration measurements were retrieved.\\n\\nThe label\u2019s **Clinical Considerations** state that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reported decreases during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The returned passage does not provide concentration values, gestational-stage measurements, clearance estimates, or a complete human pharmacokinetic dataset. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nA naturalistic study of **60 mothers** measured psychotropic-medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk and followed exposed children for the first 12 months. Its abstract reported a high breastmilk concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but this is lactation exposure evidence\u2014not a measurement of fetal exposure\u2014and the retrieved abstract does not provide a numeric lamotrigine concentration. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)\\n\\n### Observed fetal and infant outcomes\\n\\nThe selected DailyMed label reports the following registry findings for **first-trimester lamotrigine monotherapy**:\\n\\n- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2% of 1,558 infants**; 95% CI 1.6%\u20133.1%.\\n- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0% of 1,562 infants**.\\n- EURAP: major birth defects in **2.9% of 2,514 exposures**; 95% CI 2.3%\u20133.7%.\\n\\nThe label separately reports that the NAAED Pregnancy Registry observed isolated oral clefts among **2,200 infants exposed early in pregnancy** at **3.2 per 1,000**; it describes this as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls. The label also states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. A European case-control analysis reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45**; 95% CI 0.8\u20132.63. These are separate source findings and should not be combined into one estimate. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nThe label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. It states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions. The retrieved extract does not provide the underlying meta-analysis study counts or detailed results; those fields are missing in the returned material. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nA completed EUROCAT registry record states in its summary that the study found no statistically significant increased risk of oral clefts compared with other defects after in-utero lamotrigine exposure. The record has no posted results, so the registry summary is not a substitute for a full results report. [S4](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01055327)\\n\\nThe naturalistic study of 60 mothers reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborns and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. The retrieved abstract does not provide a lamotrigine-specific analysis for those outcomes. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)\\n\\n### Maternal pharmacokinetic evidence\\n\\n- **Clinical Considerations:** The label reports possible pregnancy-related changes in lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, decreased concentrations during pregnancy, and restoration toward pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. These are source-label statements, not individualized treatment instructions. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n- **Literature:** A pregnancy review states that physiological changes affect antiseizure-medication levels and discusses serum-concentration monitoring, but the retrieved abstract does not provide lamotrigine-specific numerical PK results. [S20](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)\\n- A review specifically covering lamotrigine pharmacokinetics in pregnancy was retrieved, but its abstract describes the review scope and does not report lamotrigine-specific numerical PK findings. request.question: Prepare a pregnancy evidence brief for lamotrigine. Distinguish effects on the pregnant person, fetal exposure, and fetal outcomes. ## Pregnancy evidence brief: lamotrigine

**Identity:** The requested ingredient was matched exactly to lamotrigine. [S27](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)

### Effects on the pregnant person

**Lamotrigine-specific maternal clinical effects:** No maternal adverse-effect findings specific to lamotrigine were retrieved. The selected DailyMed label’s standalone adult adverse-reaction and warning sections were missing in the returned extract; this is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that such information is absent. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

**Underlying-condition context:** The pregnancy label states that epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-drug exposure, has been associated with several maternal and obstetric outcomes. This is disease-context information, not a lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Fetal exposure

No quantitative maternal-to-fetal lamotrigine concentration measurements were retrieved.

The label’s **Clinical Considerations** state that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reported decreases during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The returned passage does not provide concentration values, gestational-stage measurements, clearance estimates, or a complete human pharmacokinetic dataset. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A naturalistic study of **60 mothers** measured psychotropic-medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk and followed exposed children for the first 12 months. Its abstract reported a high breastmilk concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but this is lactation exposure evidence—not a measurement of fetal exposure—and the retrieved abstract does not provide a numeric lamotrigine concentration. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### Observed fetal and infant outcomes

The selected DailyMed label reports the following registry findings for **first-trimester lamotrigine monotherapy**:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2% of 1,558 infants**; 95% CI 1.6%–3.1%.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0% of 1,562 infants**.
- EURAP: major birth defects in **2.9% of 2,514 exposures**; 95% CI 2.3%–3.7%.

The label separately reports that the NAAED Pregnancy Registry observed isolated oral clefts among **2,200 infants exposed early in pregnancy** at **3.2 per 1,000**; it describes this as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls. The label also states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. A European case-control analysis reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45**; 95% CI 0.8–2.63. These are separate source findings and should not be combined into one estimate. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. It states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions. The retrieved extract does not provide the underlying meta-analysis study counts or detailed results; those fields are missing in the returned material. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A completed EUROCAT registry record states in its summary that the study found no statistically significant increased risk of oral clefts compared with other defects after in-utero lamotrigine exposure. The record has no posted results, so the registry summary is not a substitute for a full results report. [S4](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01055327)

The naturalistic study of 60 mothers reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborns and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. The retrieved abstract does not provide a lamotrigine-specific analysis for those outcomes. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### Maternal pharmacokinetic evidence

- **Clinical Considerations:** The label reports possible pregnancy-related changes in lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, decreased concentrations during pregnancy, and restoration toward pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. These are source-label statements, not individualized treatment instructions. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
- **Literature:** A pregnancy review states that physiological changes affect antiseizure-medication levels and discusses serum-concentration monitoring, but the retrieved abstract does not provide lamotrigine-specific numerical PK results. [S20](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)
- A review specifically covering lamotrigine pharmacokinetics in pregnancy was retrieved, but its abstract describes the review scope and does not report lamotrigine-specific numerical PK findings. [S21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33573557/)
- The 60-mother naturalistic study measured serum and breastmilk concentrations, but the retrieved abstract does not provide numeric lamotrigine concentration values or fetal concentrations. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

**Interpretation of the retrieved PK evidence:** The returned material supports a reported change in maternal lamotrigine concentrations across pregnancy and postpartum, but does not supply a complete, lamotrigine-specific human PK dataset or an individualized concentration target.

### FAERS report-only context

For the query of lamotrigine reports containing the reaction term “foetal exposure during pregnancy,” returned reporting volumes included:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| FOETAL EXPOSURE DURING PREGNANCY | 3,527 |
| ATRIAL SEPTAL DEFECT | 357 |
| CONGENITAL ANOMALY | 327 |
| PREMATURE BABY | 257 |
| VENTRICULAR SEPTAL DEFECT | 205 |
| PATENT DUCTUS ARTERIOSUS | 153 |
| SPINA BIFIDA | 143 |
| HYPOSPADIAS | 135 |

These are spontaneous-report volumes for the stated query, not incidence rates, confirmed clinical outcomes, or proof of causation. The returned source population was not established and exposure denominators were unavailable; the results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to lamotrigine. [S2](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S14](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

The search nevertheless does not establish exhaustive literature coverage. | **ClinicalTrials.gov** | **4 matches** | Four registrations matched `daridorexant AND (pregnancy)`. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/) | It does not establish posted results, enrollment, outcomes, or confirmed age-band applicability. |
| **DailyMed** | **1 match** | One name-matched product label was returned. [S2](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/) | It does not establish population-specific sections, current FDA approval, or independent evidence. |
| **LactMed** | **Not applicable; no count** | LactMed is lactation-only. | It is not pregnancy or general pediatric evidence. |
| **MPRINT Gold snapshot** | **0 rows; 0 distinct PMIDs** | No literal daridorexant-name row matches were found in the selected MPRINT Gold snapshot tables. Snapshot date: **November 17, 2026**. No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Sertraline during lactation\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n\\nLactMed reports numeric **milk concentrations** from several small studies:\\n\\n- **45 mcg/L**; range **7\u2013207 mcg/L**, from a pooled analysis of 15 mothers.\\n- **Sertraline: 129 mcg/L**; range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**, and **norsertraline: 258 mcg/L**; range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**, from extensive 24-hour milk sampling in 26 women.\\n- **Sertraline: 26.4 mcg/L** and **norsertraline: 29 mcg/L** in a report of four mothers sampled at two months postpartum.\\n- In a report involving a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L sertraline** and **358 mcg/L norsertraline** across three randomly timed samples.\\n- **29 mcg/L** in one participant, with sampling times unspecified.\\n- **58 mcg/L** in three participants, with sampling times unspecified.\\n- **26 mcg/L in foremilk** and **46 mcg/L in hindmilk**, sampled 13 hours after a dose.\\n- **<5 mcg/L** in one first-week postpartum trough sample; among eight other women in that report, milk concentrations ranged from **11.1\u201324.5 mcg/L**.\\n- Median concentration **11.3 mcg/L**, range **3.6\u201335.7 mcg/L**, in six women providing random milk samples; the source notes that timing may affect accuracy.\\n- Average concentration **87 mcg/L**, range **12\u2013288 mcg/L**, in 15 mothers providing samples at prespecified times.\\n\\nThese are measured milk concentrations, not infant outcomes and not treatment instructions. The retrieved LactMed extract does not provide a complete infant-level concentration section; infant-level information is therefore incomplete in this extract. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\nReported findings include:\\n\\n- One **4-month-old infant** had benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation in a case report. The retrieved passage does not establish that sertraline caused these findings. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a study of **26 infants**, no acute adverse reactions were detected during the study period. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)\\n- In a study of **14 mother\u2013infant pairs**, infant whole-blood serotonin measurements were similar before and after maternal treatment; the report states that none of the infants experienced adverse effects. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)\\n- In a follow-up of **25 infants**, reported six-month weight gain was normal according to national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)\\n- No clinical adverse reactions were noted in a study of **six infants aged 5\u201334 weeks**. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/)\\n- No adverse effects were reported in **seven 4-week-old infants** in another report. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367055/)\\n- A small study compared pain responses among infants of mothers with depression who had prenatal and/or breastfeeding SSRI exposure with infants of nondepressed, unexposed mothers. Four of 30 exposed infants received sertraline, and the exposed group had blunted pain responses. Because the comparison group did not consist of depressed mothers without medication, the retrieved source states that the role of maternal depression-related factors could not be ruled out. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)\\n- An uncontrolled online survey of 930 breastfeeding mothers using antidepressants reported infant discontinuation-type symptoms in about 10% of infants overall; the result was not sertraline-specific and included pregnancy and lactation exposure groups. [S21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20807106/)\\n- A case report described a **preterm infant born at 33 weeks** who developed hyperthermia, abnormal muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying. The report also described infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite and attributed the event to serotonergic overstimulation associated with persistently high infant levels and reduced metabolism. This was a single case report involving prematurity and cannot establish frequency or risk in other infants. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)\\n\\nThe infant-outcome section in the retrieved LactMed record was truncated, so additional reported findings may be missing. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Lactation-related findings in the breastfeeding parent\\n\\nLactMed describes a report in which six patients reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; the extract does not provide their administered regimens. It also describes a small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake inhibitors in which only one participant took sertraline; the study reported delayed onset of milk secretory activation among the inhibitor-exposed group, but no statistically significant difference in feeding difficulties after day four. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nOther cited studies concerned antidepressants or SSRIs as groups rather than sertraline alone. Their breastfeeding outcomes therefore should not be treated as sertraline-specific. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThe DailyMed label retrieved was for **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, effective November 5, 2026. Its lactation section states that published literature shows low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk, reports a pooled analysis of 53 mother\u2013infant pairs with no observed adverse reactions, and states that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. The exact product match was not confirmed. The retrieved label extract included the adverse-reactions and lactation sections but did not include the expected warnings, warnings-and-precautions, boxed-warning, or drug-interactions sections; this lookup therefore cannot be treated as a complete label extract. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n\\n### Evidence limitations and context\\n\\n- The LactMed evidence base includes small reports and studies described in the record as case reports, observational studies, and a meta-analysis; the total number of studies is not established in the retrieved extract. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The retrieved evidence combines different infant ages, breastfeeding extent, and term or preterm populations. Findings from the preterm case should not be generalized to all breastfed infants. request.question: Give a balanced research summary of sertraline during lactation, with adverse findings and the relevant source context together. Distinguish observed infant outcomes from milk measurements, describe limits in study size or design, and prepare questions for a clinician. No treatment decisions.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during lactation

### Measured exposure

LactMed reports numeric **milk concentrations** from several small studies:

- **45 mcg/L**; range **7–207 mcg/L**, from a pooled analysis of 15 mothers.
- **Sertraline: 129 mcg/L**; range **11–938 mcg/L**, and **norsertraline: 258 mcg/L**; range **20–1,498 mcg/L**, from extensive 24-hour milk sampling in 26 women.
- **Sertraline: 26.4 mcg/L** and **norsertraline: 29 mcg/L** in a report of four mothers sampled at two months postpartum.
- In a report involving a preterm infant, milk concentrations averaged **201 mcg/L sertraline** and **358 mcg/L norsertraline** across three randomly timed samples.
- **29 mcg/L** in one participant, with sampling times unspecified.
- **58 mcg/L** in three participants, with sampling times unspecified.
- **26 mcg/L in foremilk** and **46 mcg/L in hindmilk**, sampled 13 hours after a dose.
- **<5 mcg/L** in one first-week postpartum trough sample; among eight other women in that report, milk concentrations ranged from **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**.
- Median concentration **11.3 mcg/L**, range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**, in six women providing random milk samples; the source notes that timing may affect accuracy.
- Average concentration **87 mcg/L**, range **12–288 mcg/L**, in 15 mothers providing samples at prespecified times.

These are measured milk concentrations, not infant outcomes and not treatment instructions. The retrieved LactMed extract does not provide a complete infant-level concentration section; infant-level information is therefore incomplete in this extract. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

Reported findings include:

- One **4-month-old infant** had benign sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation in a case report. The retrieved passage does not establish that sertraline caused these findings. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a study of **26 infants**, no acute adverse reactions were detected during the study period. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- In a study of **14 mother–infant pairs**, infant whole-blood serotonin measurements were similar before and after maternal treatment; the report states that none of the infants experienced adverse effects. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)
- In a follow-up of **25 infants**, reported six-month weight gain was normal according to national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)
- No clinical adverse reactions were noted in a study of **six infants aged 5–34 weeks**. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/)
- No adverse effects were reported in **seven 4-week-old infants** in another report. [S17](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367055/)
- A small study compared pain responses among infants of mothers with depression who had prenatal and/or breastfeeding SSRI exposure with infants of nondepressed, unexposed mothers. Four of 30 exposed infants received sertraline, and the exposed group had blunted pain responses. Because the comparison group did not consist of depressed mothers without medication, the retrieved source states that the role of maternal depression-related factors could not be ruled out. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)
- An uncontrolled online survey of 930 breastfeeding mothers using antidepressants reported infant discontinuation-type symptoms in about 10% of infants overall; the result was not sertraline-specific and included pregnancy and lactation exposure groups. [S21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20807106/)
- A case report described a **preterm infant born at 33 weeks** who developed hyperthermia, abnormal muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying. The report also described infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite and attributed the event to serotonergic overstimulation associated with persistently high infant levels and reduced metabolism. This was a single case report involving prematurity and cannot establish frequency or risk in other infants. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)

The infant-outcome section in the retrieved LactMed record was truncated, so additional reported findings may be missing. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Lactation-related findings in the breastfeeding parent

LactMed describes a report in which six patients reported decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; the extract does not provide their administered regimens. It also describes a small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake inhibitors in which only one participant took sertraline; the study reported delayed onset of milk secretory activation among the inhibitor-exposed group, but no statistically significant difference in feeding difficulties after day four. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

Other cited studies concerned antidepressants or SSRIs as groups rather than sertraline alone. Their breastfeeding outcomes therefore should not be treated as sertraline-specific. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The DailyMed label retrieved was for **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, effective November 5, 2026. Its lactation section states that published literature shows low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk, reports a pooled analysis of 53 mother–infant pairs with no observed adverse reactions, and states that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. The exact product match was not confirmed. The retrieved label extract included the adverse-reactions and lactation sections but did not include the expected warnings, warnings-and-precautions, boxed-warning, or drug-interactions sections; this lookup therefore cannot be treated as a complete label extract. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Evidence limitations and context

- The LactMed evidence base includes small reports and studies described in the record as case reports, observational studies, and a meta-analysis; the total number of studies is not established in the retrieved extract. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The retrieved evidence combines different infant ages, breastfeeding extent, and term or preterm populations. Findings from the preterm case should not be generalized to all breastfed infants. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- A case report can describe a possible adverse event but cannot estimate how often it occurs. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- “No adverse effects observed” in small studies does not establish that uncommon or long-term effects are absent.
- Milk concentration is an exposure measurement, not proof of an infant clinical effect or proof of safety.
- The LactMed record was revised August 15, 2026; its retrieved package was published October 22, 2026, and the record notes that LactMed updates monthly. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)[S3](https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pub/litarch/file_list.csv)
- The source context notes that maternal illness and treatment changes may also affect breastfeeding outcomes; this is context for interpretation, not a treatment recommendation. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)[S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Questions for a clinician or pharmacist

1. Which findings apply to the infant’s age, gestational age, prematurity status, health conditions, and degree of breastfeeding?
2. Which evidence measures milk exposure, and which evidence reports an observed infant outcome?
3. Does the retrieved product label match the exact product and formulation?
4. Are there co-exposures or prenatal exposures that affect interpretation of any infant finding?
5. What information about feeding, sleep, behavior, growth, or development would be useful to review clinically?
6. What longer-term outcomes have actually been studied, and in what populations?
7. How should the parent’s underlying condition and the risks associated with changing treatment be considered alongside the lactation evidence?

Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss any treatment change with the prescribing clinician.

Application limits:
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

No treatment decisions.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence\\n\\n**Evidence retrieved:** This is a bounded evidence brief, not a systematic review. The selected DailyMed record is **\u201cLAMOTRIGINE KIT (LAMOTRIGINE) KIT LAMOTRIGINE TABLET [OWP PHARMACEUTICALS, INC.]\u201d**, SPL version 15, effective October 12, 2026. The pregnancy text was truncated in one returned extract; structured pregnancy fields were available. The selected record is one product label, not all lamotrigine formulations. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\n### Maternal effects and underlying disease\\n\\nThe label distinguishes **disease-associated maternal/embryofetal risk** from medication exposure. It states that epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-medication exposure, has been associated with preeclampsia, preterm labor, antepartum and postpartum hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. It also states that maternal or fetal injury may be greatest with untreated or poorly controlled convulsive seizures. These are label-described risks associated with epilepsy, not lamotrigine-specific adverse outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)\\n\\nThe retrieved label extract did not contain the selected product\u2019s standalone adult adverse-reaction, warnings, or warnings-and-precautions sections; those sections are **missing in the exported data**. Therefore, maternal adverse effects cannot be comprehensively summarized from this label extract.\\n\\nA pregnancy review describes the evidence base as relying substantially on pregnancy registries, cohort studies, case-control studies, and prospective cohorts because no large randomized safety trials were identified for this subgroup. Its population was people with epilepsy during pregnancy and lactation; the design label in the returned record was **review**, not a primary outcome study. [S24](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)\\n\\n### Maternal pharmacokinetic context\\n\\nThe label reports that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. This is label context for clinician discussion, not an individualized dosing recommendation. The label distinguishes **disease-associated maternal/embryofetal risk** from medication exposure. It states that epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-medication exposure, has been associated with preeclampsia, preterm labor, antepartum and postpartum hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. It also states that maternal or fetal injury may be greatest with untreated or poorly controlled convulsive seizures. These are label-described risks associated with epilepsy, not lamotrigine-specific adverse outcomes. Its population was people with epilepsy during pregnancy and lactation; the design label in the returned record was **review**, not a primary outcome study. The label reports that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. This is label context for clinician discussion, not an individualized dosing recommendation. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

{"answer": "## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence

**Evidence retrieved:** This is a bounded evidence brief, not a systematic review. The selected DailyMed record is **“LAMOTRIGINE KIT (LAMOTRIGINE) KIT LAMOTRIGINE TABLET [OWP PHARMACEUTICALS, INC.]”**, SPL version 15, effective October 12, 2026. The pregnancy text was truncated in one returned extract; structured pregnancy fields were available. The selected record is one product label, not all lamotrigine formulations. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Maternal effects and underlying disease

The label distinguishes **disease-associated maternal/embryofetal risk** from medication exposure. It states that epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-medication exposure, has been associated with preeclampsia, preterm labor, antepartum and postpartum hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. It also states that maternal or fetal injury may be greatest with untreated or poorly controlled convulsive seizures. These are label-described risks associated with epilepsy, not lamotrigine-specific adverse outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The retrieved label extract did not contain the selected product’s standalone adult adverse-reaction, warnings, or warnings-and-precautions sections; those sections are **missing in the exported data**. Therefore, maternal adverse effects cannot be comprehensively summarized from this label extract.

A pregnancy review describes the evidence base as relying substantially on pregnancy registries, cohort studies, case-control studies, and prospective cohorts because no large randomized safety trials were identified for this subgroup. Its population was people with epilepsy during pregnancy and lactation; the design label in the returned record was **review**, not a primary outcome study. [S24](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)

### Maternal pharmacokinetic context

The label reports that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, with reports of decreased concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. This is label context for clinician discussion, not an individualized dosing recommendation. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Fetal or infant exposure

The retrieved pregnancy material did not provide a verified numeric fetal lamotrigine concentration. A separate returned study included a naturalistic sample of **60 mothers**, measured psychopharmacologic medications in serum and breast milk at different time points, and followed exposed children during the first 12 months. The abstract reported a high breast-milk concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but did not provide a numeric lamotrigine milk concentration in the returned text. This is lactation exposure information, not a measured fetal concentration. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

The returned record did not establish infant-level lamotrigine specimen results for this study. Any infant-level exposure detail is therefore **missing in the exported data**.

### Observed fetal and infant outcomes

For **first-trimester lamotrigine monotherapy** exposures, the label reports:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2% of 1,558 infants**; 95% CI 1.6%–3.1%.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0% of 1,562 infants**.
- EURAP: major birth defects in **2.9% of 2,514 exposures**; 95% CI 2.3%–3.7%.

The label states that the frequency of major congenital malformations was similar to estimates from the general population. These source populations were pregnancy-registry populations, predominantly involving women with epilepsy, and the reported exposures were lamotrigine monotherapy. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

For isolated oral clefts, the NAAED registry reported **3.2 per 1,000 among 2,200 infants** exposed early in pregnancy, described in the label as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls; 95% CI 1.4–6.3. The label states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. A European case-control study based on 21 congenital-anomaly registries reported an adjusted odds ratio of 1.45; 95% CI 0.8–2.63. These are separate source findings with different comparators and populations. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small for gestational age, and neurodevelopmental delay. It reports no data suggesting increased risk of these outcomes with lamotrigine monotherapy, while stating that differences in outcome definition, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit conclusions. This is a label summary; the returned extract did not provide the meta-analyses’ study counts or full study-population details. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A separate study of psychotropic medications included pregnancy, lactation, neonate, and child populations; its abstract reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborns and no significant developmental differences during the first 12 months. The returned abstract did not establish a lamotrigine-specific sample size or lamotrigine-specific outcome estimate, so those findings should not be generalized as lamotrigine-only results. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

Animal findings in the label included developmental toxicity, neurobehavioral abnormalities, offspring mortality, and decreased fetal folate concentrations in rats and other animals. These are animal findings and are not observed human fetal or infant outcomes. [S10](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)
